Guide

Which Essential Oils Are Phototoxic

Last updated 26 October 2026

The one essential oil hazard that can leave marks lasting months — and it comes almost entirely from citrus oils people assume are harmless.

Most essential oil safety is about irritation: use less, dilute more, patch-test. Phototoxicity is different. It is the one hazard where you can do everything right, feel nothing at the time, and still end up with dark patches that take months to fade.

It also comes from the oils people assume are safest. Citrus smells friendly. Lemon, bergamot and lime do not read as risky the way clove does.

What is actually happening

Certain cold-pressed citrus oils contain furocoumarins — bergapten is the one usually named. On skin these react with UV light. The reaction needs both: the oil alone is fine, sunlight alone is fine, together they can burn and leave lasting pigmentation.

The timing is what catches people out. You apply a blend in the morning, notice nothing, go outside at lunch, and the reaction develops hours later. Nothing about it points back at the bottle.

The oils, and their limits

These are the phototoxic oils in our range. The limit is the maximum on skin that will see direct sun within about twelve hours.

OilBotanical nameExtractionLimit on sun-exposed skin
Bergamot Citrus bergamia Cold pressed 0.4%
Lime Citrus aurantifolia Cold pressed 0.7%
Lemon Clarity Citrus limon Cold pressed 2%
Pink Grapefruit Citrus paradisi Cold pressed 4%

Two patterns are worth noticing. Steam-distilled citrus oils are not phototoxic — distillation leaves the furocoumarins behind. And sweet orange and mandarin are the exceptions among cold-pressed oils, which is why we recommend those for daytime skin blends.

How to use them anyway

  • Diffusing is unaffected. This is a skin-and-sunlight reaction; it has nothing to do with scenting a room.
  • Use them on skin in the evening, or on skin that stays covered.
  • Wash the area before going out if you have applied something citrus-heavy.
  • Rinse-off products are far lower risk than leave-on ones — the contact time is short.
  • Look for FCF or bergapten-free bergamot if you specifically want a daytime skin blend.

Twelve hours is the rough window. If skin will see direct sun within half a day, treat the limits above as firm.
